title: William III of England
description: King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1689 to 1702
wiki_lead:
William III and II (William Henry; Dutch: Willem Hendrik; 4 November 1650 – 8 March 1702), also known as William of Orange, was the sovereign Prince of Orange from birth, Stadtholder of Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, Guelders, and Overijssel in the Dutch Republic from 1672, and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1689 until his death in 1702. He ruled England, Scotland, and Ireland with his wife, Queen Mary II, until her death in 1694; their joint reign is known as that of William and Mary.
William was the only child of William II, Prince of Orange, and Mary, Princess Royal, the daughter of King Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland. His father died before his birth, making William III the prince of Orange from birth. In 1677, he married his first cousin Mary, the elder daughter of his maternal uncle James, Duke of York (later King James II).
When the Catholic French king Louis XIV attacked the Dutch Republic in 1672, William rose to power and became Louis's greatest obstacle. He made it his life's mission to oppose Louis and waged many campaigns against Louis's armies. He reorganised the Dutch army, restoring its effectiveness after the disasters of the Rampjaar and transforming it into one of the most experienced and professional forces in Europe. Convinced that the expansionist policies of Louis XIV threatened the European balance of power, William devoted much of his career to resisting French hegemony.
Many Protestants heralded William as a champion of their faith. In 1685, his Catholic uncle and father-in-law, James, became king of England, Scotland, and Ireland. James's reign was unpopular with British Protestants, who opposed James's use of rule by decree, Catholic emancipation, and a Catholic succession to the throne. Supported by a group of influential English political and religious leaders, William invaded England with a Dutch force in November 1688. He landed at the south-western English port of Brixham and James was deposed shortly afterward. After occupying London he was swiftly offered the crown alongside his wife Mary. The event would be known as the Glorious Revolution, leading to the adoption of the English Bill of Rights.
During the early years of his reign, William was occupied abroad with the Nine Years' War (1688–1697), leaving Mary to govern the three kingdoms. She died in 1694. In 1696, the Jacobites, a faction loyal to the deposed James, plotted unsuccessfully to assassinate William and restore James to the throne. In Scotland, William's role in ordering the Massacre of Glencoe remains notorious. William's lack of children and the death in 1700 of his nephew the Duke of Gloucester threatened the Protestant succession. The danger was averted by placing William and Mary's cousins, the Protestant House of Hanover, in line to the throne after Mary's sister Anne with the Act of Settlement 1701. Upon his death in 1702, William was succeeded in his kingdoms by Anne and as titular Prince of Orange by his cousin John William Friso.

Early life


Birth and family

William III and II was born on 4 November 1650 in The Hague in the Dutch Republic. Baptised William Henry (Dutch: Willem Hendrik), he was the only child of Mary, Princess Royal, and stadtholder William II, Prince of Orange. Mary was the elder daughter of King Charles I of England, Scotland and Ireland and sister of kings Charles II and James II and VII.
Eight days before William was born, his father died of smallpox; thus, William was the sovereign Prince of Orange from the moment of his birth. Immediately, a conflict arose between his mother and his paternal grandmother, Amalia of Solms-Braunfels, over the name to be given to the infant. Mary wanted to name him Charles after her brother, but her mother-in-law insisted on giving him the name William (Willem) to bolster his prospects of becoming stadtholder. grok_lead: William III (4 November 1650 â 8 March 1702) was a Dutch prince who served as Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic from 1672 and later became king of England, Scotland, and Ireland, reigning jointly with his wife Mary II from 1689 until her death in 1694 and solely thereafter until his own death. Born in The Hague as the only child of William II, Prince of Orange, and Mary Stuart (daughter of England 's Charles I), he was orphaned shortly after birth and raised amid political turmoil in the Netherlands. Ascending to the stadtholdership at age 22 during the French invasion of 1672âknown as the Rampjaar âhe rallied Dutch forces to resist Louis XIV's expansionism, forging a lifelong commitment to countering French hegemony. In 1677, he married his first cousin Mary, the Protestant daughter of the Catholic James II, positioning him as a key figure in English opposition to absolutist rule. Invited by English nobles fearing Catholic succession, William led an amphibious invasion of England in November 1688 with 15,000 troops, prompting James II's flight and the bloodless Glorious Revolution that installed William and Mary as joint monarchs under a Declaration of Rights limiting royal prerogative. His reign prioritized grand alliances against France, including the Nine Years' War (1688â1697), where English and Dutch forces under his command checked Louis XIV's ambitions, though at great fiscal cost, culminating in the Treaty of Ryswick. A staunch Protestant and military leader, William's policies entrenched parliamentary sovereignty and balanced European power, but faced Jacobite resistance and domestic criticism over war expenditures and his Dutch favoritism. He died childless from pneumonia following a broken collarbone sustained in a riding accident, succeeded by Mary's sister Anne.
